nameStory: The spotted snake millipede gets its name from the distinctive row of reddish or orange spots running along each side of its pale, elongated body. When disturbed, it coils up like a tiny snake, and its smooth, cylindrical form definitely resembles a miniature serpent as it glides through the soil.
description: The spotted snake millipede is a small, slender millipede that looks like a tiny white or pale yellow snake with colorful spots. These introduced European millipedes are quite small, typically reaching about half an inch to an inch in length. Unlike their larger, darker cousins, spotted snake millipedes have a smooth, almost translucent appearance that makes them stand out against dark soil. They're part of the "thin snake millipede" family, and true to their name, they're much more delicate-looking than the chunky millipedes you might find under logs.

idTips.label: Distinctive spots
idTips.description: Look for a row of bright reddish-orange or pink spots running down each side of the body - these spots are actually scent glands and are the millipede's most recognizable feature

idTips.label: Pale coloration
idTips.description: The body is creamy white to pale yellow, often with a slightly translucent quality that lets you see internal structures

idTips.label: Snake-like movement
idTips.description: Moves in smooth, flowing motions rather than the more segmented gait of larger millipedes, and coils up tightly when threatened

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Much smaller than most millipedes you'll encounter, about as thick as a pencil lead and rarely longer than your thumbnail

idTips.label: Smooth texture
idTips.description: Body feels smooth and somewhat soft to the touch, lacking the hard, armor-like segments of larger millipede species

habitat: Look for spotted snake millipedes in rich, moist soil in gardens, compost areas, and disturbed ground where organic matter is abundant. They're particularly fond of areas around greenhouses, nurseries, and well-fertilized garden beds. Since they're an introduced species, they're most commonly found in developed areas rather than deep wilderness.

seasonality.spring: Most active as soil warms up and moisture levels are high from snowmelt and spring rains. This is when you're most likely to spot them moving through garden soil.
seasonality.summer: Continue to be active but may go deeper into soil during hot, dry spells. Look for them in consistently moist areas like compost piles or under mulch.
seasonality.fall: Active again with cooler temperatures and increased moisture, often seen when turning over garden soil or moving plant debris.
seasonality.winter: Retreat deep into soil or compost to avoid freezing, rarely visible at the surface except during mild spells.

funFact: Despite being called a "snake" millipede, these tiny creatures actually have between 30-50 pairs of legs, meaning a single individual can have up to 100 legs working together to create that smooth, serpentine gliding motion!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small earthworms, but millipedes have distinct segments, many tiny legs, and those telltale orange spots along the sides. Remember: if it has spots and coils up when poked, it's the spotted snake millipede - earthworms just squirm without coiling.
contextualKnowledge: This is an introduced species from Europe that has established itself in North American gardens and disturbed soils. While some people worry about non-native species, spotted snake millipedes are generally harmless decomposers that help break down organic matter, though they can occasionally nibble on plant roots in large numbers.
compareHints: The spotted snake millipede is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it relatively easy to identify once you know what to look for. Compared to other thin millipedes in the region, it's distinguished by its pale coloration and bright spots - most other small millipedes tend to be darker brown or gray without the distinctive spotted pattern.
